title: Quod Idola Dii non sint
author: Cyprian
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0104a.stoa006.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: ceterum Mars Thracius et Iuppiter Creticus et Iuno uel Argiua uel Samia uel Poena et Diana Taurica et deum mater Idaea et Aegyptia portenta, non numina: quae utique si quid potestatis habuissent, sua ac suorum regna seruassent. plane sunt apud Romanos et uicti penates, quos Aeneas profugus aduexit: est et Venus calua, multo hic turpius calua, quam apud Homerum uulnerata.
passages.english: As for the rest, there are Thracian Mars, Cretan Jupiter, Juno whether of Argos or of Samos or the Punic one, Taurian Diana, the Idaean mother of the gods, and the Egyptian monstrosities, [which are] portents, not divinities. Certainly, if these had had any power, they would have preserved their own kingdoms and those of their people. Among the Romans there are, to be sure, also the conquered Penates, which Aeneas brought with him as a fugitive. There is also the Bald Venus, far more shamefully bald here than she was wounded in Homer.
passages.notes: 'Poena' is taken as 'Poena' = Punic (i.e. Carthaginian Juno); some editions read 'Poena' differently. 'Venus calua' refers to the Roman cult of Venus Calva.

passages.original: hos et poetae daemonas norunt et Socrates instrui se et regi ad arbitrium daemonii praedicabat, et magis inde est ad perniciosa uel ludicra potentatus: quorum tamen praecipuus Ostanes et formam ueri Dei negat conspici posse et angelos ueros sedi eius dicit adsistere. in quo et Plato pari ratione consentit et unum Deum seruans ceteros angelos uel daemonas dicit. Hermes quoque Trismegistus unum Deum loquitur eumque inconprehensibilem adque inaestimabilem confitetur.
passages.english: The poets too know these as *daemones* [spirits], and Socrates declared that he was instructed and governed at the will of a *daemonium* [divine spirit], and from this source the magi have their power for harmful or frivolous [works]. Yet the foremost of these, Ostanes, both denies that the form of the true God can be seen and says that true angels stand beside his throne. In this Plato also agrees on the same reasoning, and, maintaining one God, he calls the rest angels or *daemones*. Hermes Trismegistus too speaks of one God and confesses him to be incomprehensible and beyond estimation.
passages.notes: 'magis' is read as 'magis' = to the magi (dative of magus), not the adverb 'more'; the sentence is otherwise awkward. 'potentatus' is taken as the noun 'power'.
